title: New Maryland state park, complete with yurts and cabins, set to open late this summer
summary: After spending $8.7 million to buy it, and another $800,000 to renovate it, state officials are looking forward to the late summer opening of a unique resort in Savage River State Forest boasting a lodge, cabins and yurts for visitors.
content:
by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters February 8, 2026

by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters February 8, 2026

In the mid-1990s, Mike Dreisbach and his wife Jan purchased a patch of forest in Garrett County with the dream of opening a wilderness retreat.

Some thirty years later, their land, now featuring a woodsy lodge, and a network of cabins and yurts, is set to be reopened as one of Maryland’s next — and perhaps most unique — state parks. An opening is planned for late August, state officials say.

“We leveraged our lives and created something that was pretty phenomenal,” said Dreisbach, 75. “I have complete faith in Maryland … It will be one of the greatest parks in the state.”

Dreisbach said that the couple had a higher bid from a Pennsylvania-based investment firm, but opted to sell the land to the state, in hopes that the small woodland resort they built outside of Frostburg would retain its character.

“That was 30 years of our life, from dreaming, to building, to running it,” Dreisbach said. “We wanted to turn it over to somebody that would not screw it up.”

The 42-acre property, formerly known as Savage River Lodge, is nestled within Savage River State Forest, meaning the state has secured a much-desired privately held parcel that interrupted the state land, known in park ranger parlance as an “in-holding.”

“You really worry, if it were to change hands to another private operation, what could happen to that in-holding?” asked Sarah Milbourne, western region manager at the Maryland Park Service. “So this was such a do-not-miss opportunity for us.”

Ever since the state purchased the property in December 2024 for $8.7 million, Maryland Park Service officials say park rangers and contractors have been hurriedly completing maintenance and repair projects on the aging buildings and the grounds.

Replacing the lodge roof. Remediating a bat infestation. Repairing siding and painting decks. Removing hazardous trees and invasive vegetation. Adding primitive camp sites tucked into the forest.

And there’s much more to come. The state plans significant repairs to the single, mile-long gravel road that leads to the property. The state expects to outfit the cabins and yurts with kitchenettes, and several need to be made accessible for people with disabilities, Milbourne said.

But state officials say that the spend — which the state Board of Public Works approved at 10% of the purchase price, or over $800,000 — will all be worth it.

When they reopen the park, christened Savage Highlands, some time around late August, they will begin offering resort-style facilities for rent — but at a considerably cheaper price, befitting that of a state park, opening the parks doors to an entirely new host of visitors.

“There aren’t a ton of opportunities in the state to have this — maybe a little upper-level — experience, where you still are nestled in a forest, so close to fly-fishing streams and so close to really great trails,” Milbourne said. “I mean, you could step out of a cabin and almost onto a trail right away.”

The exact rental cost has yet to be determined, Milbourne said, but she is confident it will be a reduction compared to when it was under private ownership, when stays could cost hundreds per night.

That said, many of the experiences once offered to lodge guests won’t be available at the new state park. The lodge once featured a restaurant and bar, for instance, which also kept cabin and yurt guests well-fed. But when the property opens to visitors later this year, it will remain shuttered.

The department is still considering whether it will operate some sort of concessions venue at the lodge, Milbourne said, but one thing is certain — that would be put out for a bid to a private contractor.

“We do a lot of things very well. Running a restaurant is not necessarily a park ranger’s forte,” Milbourne said.

The opening will also occur in phases, Milbourne said. At first, the state will open the main lodge, but only a select number of cabins and yurts for rentals. At the beginning, the park will also close during the winter months, Milbourne said, because of the condition of the road leading to the property.

To some observers, the wait-time is a signal that the property may be requiring more work than the state anticipated. Mike Gregory, who lives close to Savage Highlands and formerly served as superintendent at nearby New Germany State Park from 1994 to 2009, said he fears that the state overpaid.

“They spent an inordinate amount of money, and they will continue to spend an inordinate amount of money to make this look like a good purchase, when, in fact, it’s a white elephant,” Gregory said.

Milbourne noted that while there have been “quirks” with the property, they come with the territory of purchasing a property like Savage Lodge. She estimated that standing up a new state park in the region, which experiences a high demand for overnight stays, could cost triple what the state paid for the park.

“People were concerned about Maryland making this decision, but what we have found is that especially in Western Maryland, every one of our cabins are booked all the time and people are clamoring to get in, and clamoring to have experiences — and ones that are accessible, ones that are affordable.”

And the property, especially with its lodge, resembling one tucked beneath ski slopes, provides something unique that other Park Service properties just don’t, Milbourne said.

“When you’re driving on the road into that place, and you’re driving through some of the evergreens, I mean, you can expect to see a black bear run across the road. I’ve seen turkeys,” Milbourne said. “It’s still wild, still rustic. But again, still so comfortable and homey. To sit by the fire in that lodge after a long day — it’s just fantastic.”

Gregory said he also fears, however, that the new park will place a strain on the Park Service’s already scarce resources.

Already, the state is using field staff from New Germany to assist with the repairs, Milbourne said, though it has also pulled in staff from other parks to assist with big projects. But additional hires are planned, Milbourne said, predominantly seasonal workers.

Dreisbach said that at its peak in visitorship, which came in the wake of the coronavirus pandemic, the lodge employed some 40 people, some of them part-time and others full-time.

“We paid for a lot of college educations at Frostburg State,” he joked.

Dreisbach and his wife also lived on the property, in a home that the state obtained as part of the deal. So, these days, the duo are traveling the country in a newly purchased motor home — and visiting plenty of parks.

But one day, their travels could bring them back to their old stomping grounds, now in state hands.

“We’re looking to go back there and stay one day,” Dreisbach said.
